scenes.title: Cost Based Optimization
scenes.narration: A cost-based optimizer weighs several possible plans and chooses the one it estimates to be cheapest to run.

scenes.title: Two ways to choose a plan

left.title: Rule-based
points: Ignores how much data actually exists
Same plan regardless of table size

right.title: Cost-based
points: Picks the cheapest of many candidates

scenes.narration: A rule-based optimizer follows fixed heuristics and would pick the same plan whether a table holds ten rows or ten million. A cost-based optimizer instead estimates the cost of each candidate plan from real statistics and adapts its choice as the data changes, selecting whichever plan looks cheapest.

scenes.title: Statistics the optimizer relies on
bullets: Total row counts for each table
Histograms describing how values are distributed
Number of distinct values and index selectivity
scenes.narration: The optimizer leans on table statistics to make its estimates. It uses row counts to gauge scale, histograms to understand how values are distributed across a column, and distinct-value counts and index selectivity to judge how many rows a filter or join will actually match.

scenes.title: How the optimizer decides
steps: Parse the query and enumerate candidate plans
Estimate rows at each step using statistics
Assign a cost to CPU, I/O, and memory per plan
Execute the plan with the lowest total cost
scenes.narration: First the optimizer parses the query and enumerates candidate plans, varying join orders and access methods. Using statistics it estimates the rows produced at each step. It then assigns a cost reflecting CPU, I/O, and memory, and finally executes whichever plan carries the lowest total cost.

scenes.title: Keep statistics fresh
scenes.narration: When statistics grow stale after heavy inserts or deletes, the optimizer estimates poorly and can choose a bad plan. Running ANALYZE in PostgreSQL, or UPDATE STATISTICS in SQL Server, recomputes those statistics so the optimizer sees the table as it really is today.

scenes.text: Stale statistics are a top cause of sudden slowdowns. After large data changes, refresh them so the optimizer's cost estimates stay accurate.
scenes.narration: Stale statistics are one of the most common causes of a query that was fast yesterday and slow today. After large data changes, refresh them so the optimizer's cost estimates remain accurate.

scenes.text: Cost-based optimization turns statistics into cost estimates to pick the cheapest plan — keep statistics current and you help the optimizer help you.
scenes.narration: Cost-based optimization converts statistics into cost estimates and picks the cheapest plan, so keeping those statistics current is the simplest way to help the optimizer help you.
